articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities and Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities involved with Iran. This action aims to further restrict the Iranian regime's access to financial resources and its ability to support destabilizing activities.

In addition to the Iran designations, OFAC also released updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba. These FAQs provide guidance and clarification on existing sanctions policies related to transactions and interactions with Cuba, assisting individuals and entities in ensuring compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: OFAC has announced new designations against individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global criminal networks and protecting national security interests.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing specific authorizations related to certain transactions. Furthermore, an amended Russia-related General License and associated Frequently Asked Questions were published, offering updated guidance on sanctions pertaining to Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt the financing and support networks of terrorist organizations globally.

The designations aim to isolate these actors from the international financial system and prevent them from facilitating further acts of terrorism. This move reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to combating global terrorism through financial sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Activities
body: OFAC has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities engaged in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This dual focus highlights the interconnected nature of these illicit networks and the comprehensive approach taken by the U.S. government to combat them.

The designations aim to sever financial ties and disrupt the operations of those who facilitate the illegal drug trade and support terrorist organizations, thereby safeguarding international security and stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Listings
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update to its Iran designation listings. This action reflects ongoing adjustments to the sanctions regime targeting Iran, ensuring that the list of sanctioned individuals and entities remains current and effective.
These updates are part of the U.S. government's continuous efforts to exert pressure on the Iranian regime and address its proliferation activities and support for regional proxies.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: OFAC has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals involved in Iran-related activities. These actions are part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing behavior and its support for terrorism.
The designations aim to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and its ability to fund illicit activities, reinforcing the pressure on the regime to alter its policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions
body: OFAC has announced new designations targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations, aiming to disrupt their illicit financial activities and operations. These actions highlight the U.S. government's commitment to combating sophisticated criminal networks that pose threats to national security and the global financial system.

Additionally, OFAC imposed new designations related to Cuba and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures are part of ongoing efforts to address the Cuban government's actions and ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Amends Venezuela General License
body: OFAC has announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities and its support for regional proxies.

Furthermore, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License along with a new Frequently Asked Question. These updates aim to provide clarity and guidance to stakeholders regarding sanctions compliance for both Iran and Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This update provides specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Iranian sanctions program.
The amendment aims to refine the scope of permissible activities, ensuring that humanitarian and other authorized transactions can proceed while maintaining pressure on the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and DRC
body: OFAC has announced new designations targeting entities involved with North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to counter proliferation activities by North Korea and address human rights abuses and corruption in the DRC.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to enforcing sanctions regimes that promote international peace and security, and uphold human rights globally.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Agrees to Pay $1,529,685 for OFAC Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. This enforcement action highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally.

The penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to holding companies accountable for failing to prevent transactions with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions. Companies are reminded to conduct thorough due diligence and implement effective internal controls to mitigate sanctions risks.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of multiple U.S. sanctions programs. This settlement is part of a coordinated enforcement action that also involved significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.

The violations included failures to mitigate and report priority national security risks, such as those related to Chinese money laundering networks, illicit finance along the southwest border, and transactions implicating Iran and Russia. The bank's deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program were a key factor in the enforcement actions.

This substantial penalty serves as a reminder of the critical importance for financial institutions to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs and to address identified weaknesses promptly and effectively.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $175,015 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. This enforcement action underscores the need for logistics companies to implement stringent compliance measures.

The penalty highlights the risks associated with international shipping and the importance of screening all parties involved in a transaction against OFAC's sanctions lists. Companies in the logistics sector are urged to enhance their due diligence processes to avoid facilitating prohibited transactions.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

The substantial penalty serves as a reminder that individuals involved in facilitating or conducting transactions that violate U.S. sanctions can face significant financial consequences. Compliance with OFAC regulations is crucial for all parties engaged in international financial activities.

The penalty underscores the importance of conducting thorough due diligence on customers and end-users to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions. Even smaller violations can result in significant financial penalties.

The penalty serves as a reminder that companies providing consulting and other services must implement effective sanctions screening and compliance protocols to avoid engaging in prohibited transactions or activities involving sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Pays Record $275,000,000 OFAC Penalty

The significant fine highlights OFAC's aggressive enforcement posture and its commitment to deterring sanctions evasion globally. Companies with extensive international operations are urged to review and strengthen their compliance frameworks to prevent similar violations.

The penalty serves as a reminder that brokerage firms and other financial service providers must implement robust sanctions screening and compliance programs to identify and block transactions involving sanctioned individuals, entities, or jurisdictions.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $3,777,000 Civil Penalty to OFAC

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced an extension of the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR) titled 'Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities.' The suspension, which was set to expire on November 9, 2026, has been extended through January 10, 2027.

This final rule further stays the amendments to 15 CFR parts 732, 734, 736, 744, and 748 that were initially published on September 30, 2025, and subsequently stayed on November 10, 2025. The extension provides additional time for stakeholders to adjust to potential changes in export control regulations concerning affiliates of listed entities.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
